exam: What is the most likely underlying disease in a patient with PG? — Inflammatory bowel disease (UC or Crohn’s).
Which test would you order first to rule out infection? — Skin biopsy with culture and histology.
Why is a high‑dose steroid preferred initially? — It rapidly suppresses neutrophilic inflammation and is effective in most cases.
What complication is most feared if PG is untreated? — Secondary infection leading to sepsis.
How would you manage a PG patient who is HIV positive? — Treat HIV, use steroid sparingly, consider cyclosporine or infliximab.
What is pathergy and why is it important in PG? — Minor trauma can worsen lesions; avoid unnecessary procedures.
ai.title: Pyoderma Gangrenosum
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: A neutrophilic dermatosis presenting as painful ulceration, often linked to systemic disease. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by biopsy and exclusion of infection. Management centers on immunosuppression and wound care.

sections.p: Pyoderma gangrenosum (PG) is an immune‑mediated skin disorder that causes rapidly expanding, painful ulcers with undermined violaceous borders. Diagnosis is clinical, using the Delphi criteria: (1) rapidly progressive ulcer with violaceous border, (2) exclusion of infection, (3) histology showing neutrophilic infiltrate, and (4) association with systemic disease or a good response to steroids.

t.b: Confirm neutrophilic infiltrate and rule out infection; a sterile, dense neutrophilic dermal infiltrate supports PG.
Rule out bacterial infection; a negative result supports PG.
Elevated CRP/ESR are non‑specific but common; normal values do not exclude PG.

b: Large ulcer >10 cm = poor wound healing
sections.p: PG is staged by ulcer size and systemic involvement. The Wagner system (0–4) is useful: 0 = intact skin, 1 = superficial ulcer, 2 = deep ulcer, 3 = extensive ulcer with necrosis, 4 = gangrene. Severe disease often requires intensive care.
PG is associated with inflammatory bowel disease (UC, Crohn’s), rheumatoid arthritis, and hematologic malignancies. In East Africa, HIV, TB, and malaria can trigger or mimic PG.

t.b: Rule out HIV as a trigger; a positive result may alter immunosuppressive strategy.
Exclude TB, which can cause ulcerative lesions; a positive Mantoux or GeneXpert suggests TB.

sections.p: Patients report sudden, painful ulceration, often on lower limbs. Ulcers have a purplish undermined edge, may bleed, and can be accompanied by systemic symptoms such as fever or joint pain.
Investigations aim to exclude infection and identify underlying disease.

t.b: Look for neutrophilia or anemia; abnormal values suggest systemic disease.
Elevated values support inflammation but are non‑specific.
Identify co‑existing infections that may influence treatment.
Confirm neutrophilic infiltrate and rule out malignancy or infection.

t.a: Imaging (X‑ray/US) if deep tissue involvement suspected

sections.p: Complications include secondary infection, sepsis, and systemic organ involvement. Red flags are rapid ulcer expansion, systemic signs of sepsis, or failure to respond to antibiotics.

Treat the underlying disease first, then start systemic immunosuppression. First‑line is high‑dose prednisone; if contraindicated, cyclosporine or infliximab can be used. Supportive wound care with non‑adherent dressings and infection control is essential.

t.b: Avoid abrupt cessation to prevent flare; taper over weeks based on response.
Only if infection is proven; avoid unnecessary use to prevent resistance.

b: Monthly lab monitoring for drug toxicity
Early treatment of IBD or RA
sections.p: Regular wound assessment, monitoring for infection, and adjusting immunosuppression are key. Preventive measures include early recognition of ulceration and prompt treatment of underlying disease.

b: Cellulitis – responds to antibiotics, no undermined edge
Necrotizing fasciitis – rapid systemic toxicity, gas on imaging
Venous stasis ulcer – usually at ankle, flat border
sections.p: PG can mimic cellulitis, necrotizing fasciitis, and venous stasis ulcers. Key differences are the violaceous border and lack of response to antibiotics.

b: Normal inflammatory markers in early disease
sections.p: A negative culture does not exclude infection; low bacterial load can give false negatives. Normal CRP/ESR may occur in early PG.

whenToSeekHelp: Pain out of proportion to ulcer size
